interactions.summary: Jiang closes the meta-argument about mission, announces a jump to Cantos 11 and 12, and frames Thomas Aquinas, the Dominicans, Bonaventure, and the Franciscans as reforming forces whose eventual failure Dante wants to explain.
Carol reads the opening of Paradise Canto 11, where Dante condemns mortals whose studies and ambitions keep their thought fixed on earthly things.
Jiang asks what Dante's criticism of academic studies means, a student answers that scholars are driven by ulterior motives, and Jiang confirms the response.

speaker_notes.note: The reader is again likely Carol, continuing the reading role Jiang assigns her in this session.

claims.claim: Jiang says the platform will skip around Dante not because the omitted cantos are unimportant but because he does not yet feel able to interpret every canto fully and wants to focus on the pieces he can teach honestly.

He presents Thomas Aquinas as the second most famous Catholic theologian after Augustine and as the first European figure to reconcile classical Greek philosophy with Christian faith, though similar synthesis was already happening in the Islamic Golden Age.
Jiang characterizes the Dominicans as a pre-Jesuit order devoted to learning and education in service of enforcing Christian orthodoxy.

He presents the Franciscans as a poverty movement founded by Francis of Assisi in continuity with Jesus and the poor, and he says both the Dominican and Franciscan reforms initially seemed to restore hope to a corrupt Church before later failing.
claims.temporal_scope: Historical and interpretive framing stated on 2026-06-17.

claims.claim: Jiang identifies Dante's governing question here as why reform movements rooted in selfless knowledge or selfless spirituality begin well and still fail.
Jiang interprets Dante's attack on academic studies as a complaint that scholars use thought for earthly ambition rather than for God and truth.

signature_moments.moment: The whole canto is framed as an autopsy of reform movements that looked like Europe's hope and still failed.
signature_moments.source_phrase: why is it that these two movements, which started out great ... why did they fail?
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It names the structural problem Jiang wants Dante to solve: how selfless institutions decay.

signature_moments.moment: Dante's opening image compresses worldly professions and appetites into wings trapped low to the earth.
signature_moments.source_phrase: syllogistic reasonings that bring your wings to flight so low to earthly things
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's strongest quoted image and sets up Jiang's anti-earthbound reading of scholarship.

signature_moments.moment: Academic study is redefined as suspect when it becomes an earthly career game rather than a path toward God and truth.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It links the class's mission language to Dante's own attack on misdirected intellectual life.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The order Jiang describes as a learning-centered, orthodoxy-enforcing precursor to the Jesuits and one half of Dante's paired reform problem.
The poverty-centered order founded by Francis of Assisi that Jiang treats as the spiritual counterpart to the Dominicans in Dante's reform drama.
In Jiang's reading, the line names intellectual activity that has become earthbound and self-serving rather than oriented toward truth and God.

chronology_notes.note: This packet marks the seminar's transition on 2026-06-17 from meta-debate about the platform's mission into close reading of Paradise 11 and 12.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang's compressed historical claims about Aquinas, Europe, and the Islamic Golden Age are part of his lecture framing here and should not be treated as settled historiography without separate checking.
